questions: Can you explain in your own words what you mean when you say "The p-value measures how surprising the data would be if the null hypothesis were true"?
Could you walk me through why you say "we reject the null hypothesis. This is the standard frequentist conclusion" and what that decision implies about the null hypothesis?
What do you understand by the statement "proves conclusively that the new study method works" and how it relates to the p‑value?
How would you assess whether the "A 4.1-point difference might be meaningful in some contexts and minor in others" is practically significant for students?
What limitations do you see when you note that "generalising to all students everywhere requires caution" and how might they affect the interpretation of the test?
briefing: Based on the submission only (no practice conversation). The student correctly explains the p‑value, stating “The p-value measures how surprising the data would be if the null hypothesis were true… only a 3% chance of seeing a difference this large by chance if there were really no effect,” and appropriately rejects the null at α=0.05 (“we reject the null hypothesis”). They also acknowledge practical significance, noting “A 4.1‑point difference might be meaningful in some contexts and minor in others…”. The discussion of limitations is solid, mentioning sample size, generalisability, and t‑test assumptions (“generalising to all students everywhere requires caution… The t‑test also assumes independence and approximate normality”). However, the claim that the result “proves conclusively that the new study method works” misrepresents what a p‑value can demonstrate and shows a misconception about certainty. Overall the reasoning is mostly clear but is undermined by this over‑statement.
suggested_questions: Can you clarify why you say the p‑value “proves conclusively” that Method A works, and how that aligns with the correct interpretation of statistical significance?
How would you decide whether the 4.1‑point difference is practically important for students in this course, given the context you described?
